newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries firmer in London, swap trade active.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries firmer in London, swap trade active.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries pushed higher in London on Wednesday, bolstered by swap activity and a calmer European market, traders said.
But a two-year note sale may throw up obstacles in the U.S. session, they said.

"Swap buyers have been active this morning -- mostly in the 10-year sector," a salesman at a U.S. bank said. Ten-year Eurobond deals each worth $500 million from Associates Corp and British Columbia fuelled trade.
The benchmark long bond was quoted at 95-05 at 1027 GMT, yielding 7.017, compared with 94-31 at the close in Tokyo and New York on Tuesday.
The yield edged back over 7.0 percent in New York on Tuesday for the first time in a month as the Conference Board's consumer confidence index surged to its highest level in 28 years.
European markets settled back down on Wednesday after a surprise win by left-wing parties in French elections on Sunday left markets questioning the future of European currency union.
But the trader said the market faced a rough ride later in the session when the Treasury auctions $16.5 billion of two-year notes at 1745 GMT. A $12.0 billion five-year auction follows on Thursday.
"The short-term push here following the swaps may well be offset by domestic U.S. concerns about the auction," he said.

"When-issued turnover for us has been fairly low," he added. "We haven't seen that many customers interested in rolling forward which seems to suggest two- and five-year notes may not necessarily pull in the type of demand we need to underwrite the auction at these yield levels."
April durable goods were also due, at 1230 GMT.

Economists surveyed by Reuters showed a consensus forecast for a 1.3 percent gain after a 2.6 percent drop in March. Excluding defence, orders were expected to rise 0.8 percent after a 2.3 percent drop last time.
"This data has been a bit of a nightmare recently -- so volatile," Ian Gunner, international economist at Chase in London, said.

"The 2.6 percent drop we saw last month was a drop in the ocean compared to the gains we saw in January and February, so any sort of rise in April would be confirmation there's still an uptrend in orders," he said.
In the futures market, the June contract was quoted at 108-20 in automated trade, down 3/32 from the Chicago settlement. --Jacqueline Thorpe, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
